Work in C:\Users\edmem\kodely-prod (a Next.js 16 + Prisma app called Kodely — an AI website builder at kodely.me).

BUILD: transactional email notifications.

## Why
Kodely sends exactly one email today — the contact form (`lib/mail.ts`, `app/api/contact/**` — read both first). A user who runs out of credits, or whose build failed, or who signed up and never came back, hears nothing. The highest-value one by far is **low credits**: hitting zero mid-session with no warning is the exact bill-shock/dead-end experience this product positions against.

## Scope — YOU MAY ONLY CREATE/EDIT FILES UNDER `lib/notifications/` AND `app/api/notifications/`
Everything else is off limits — other agents are running in parallel. READ anything, especially `lib/mail.ts`, `lib/credits.ts`, `lib/events.ts`, `prisma/schema.prisma`.

## What to build
1. **`lib/notifications/templates.ts`** — plain-text-first email templates (with a simple, inlined-CSS HTML alternative; no remote images, no tracking pixels). Start with these four:
   - **Welcome** — what they can build, what a credit is, link to get started.
   - **Low credits** — fires when the balance drops below roughly two builds' worth. Must state the balance and roughly how many builds that is, and link to top up. Read `averageBuildCredits` in `lib/credits.ts` — per-user measured average is what the UI already uses, so the email must agree with the meter or it undermines it.
   - **Build failed** — reassure explicitly that they were NOT charged (that is genuinely true; verify in `app/api/generate/route.ts`), and say what to try.
   - **Site published** — the URL, and what to do next.
2. **`lib/notifications/send.ts`** — the dispatcher. Reuses the existing transport in `lib/mail.ts` (do not build a second one). Must be **fire-and-forget and non-blocking**: an email failure must never fail a build, a publish, or a signup.
3. **`app/api/notifications/run/route.ts`** — a cron-triggered endpoint for the digest-style ones (low credits). **Protect it with a shared secret from the environment** (`KODELY_CRON_SECRET`), compared in constant time; an unauthenticated endpoint that emails your entire user base is a gift to an attacker. Return 404, not 401, on a bad secret.

## The hard problem: DO NOT SEND DUPLICATES
There is **no schema change available to you** — `prisma/schema.prisma` is owned by someone else and off limits. So you cannot add a `sent_emails` table. Solve idempotency with what exists.

Strong hint: `lib/events.ts` has an append-only `Event` table with a closed `EVENTS` vocabulary — **read it, but you may not edit it**, so you cannot add an event name either. Work out what you CAN query to determine "have we already told this person this?" — e.g. deriving state from `CreditLedger`, `Build`, `Project.publishedAt`, and existing `Event` rows. If you genuinely cannot make a given email idempotent without a schema change, **do not send it** — implement it, leave it disabled behind a clear guard, and say exactly what schema you would need in your report. I will add it.

Emailing someone "you're running low" every hour is worse than never emailing them at all.

## Critical constraints
- **Never email anyone content that isn't theirs**, and never put credentials, tokens, session ids, or prompt text in an email.
- **No unsubscribe mechanism exists.** These must all be genuinely transactional (triggered by the user's own account state), never marketing. Do not build a re-engagement or drip campaign — that needs consent tracking we don't have. Say so in your report if you're tempted.
- DO NOT modify: prisma/schema.prisma, lib/mail.ts, lib/credits.ts, lib/events.ts, lib/agent.ts, lib/agent-sdk.ts, anything else under lib/ outside lib/notifications/, app/api/** outside app/api/notifications/, app/**, proxy.ts, deploy.sh, .env, package.json.
- DO NOT add npm dependencies (nodemailer is already present).
- DO NOT run `npm run build`, `git commit`, `git push`, or `deploy.sh`. **Do not actually send email to any real address.**
- Run `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint app lib components`; BOTH must be clean — the repo is at zero lint errors and must stay there.
- You may query the local Postgres read-only to check your idempotency queries. Do not modify data.

## Report back
The four templates, exactly how you made each one idempotent (or why you disabled it), the env vars needed, the cron line to schedule it, what you verified vs. assumed, and any schema you'd want me to add.

18	  email            String   @unique
19	  // Nullable because a Google-only account never sets a local password.
20	  passwordHash     String?
21	  googleId         String?  @unique

23	  role             String   @default("CUSTOMER") // CUSTOMER | ADMIN

27	  // Self-imposed ceiling on credits spent per rolling 30 days. NULL = no cap.

43	// One wide table rather than a table per dashboard, because the activation
44	// funnel, retention cohorts, per-user journey, attribution and the overview

Good, the APP_URL env var exists with a default. Now I'm wrestling with idempotency — I need a way to track whether an email was already sent, but looking at the available tables (User, Event, StripeEvent, Session, Project, ProjectFile, Message, Build, CreditLedger, BlogPost), there's no obvious place to record that state without adding a new Event name, which I'm not allowed to do since I can't edit the events definitions.

So for the welcome email specifically, since I can't hook into the signup route directly, it has to come from a cron job, and without a durable "already welcomed" record, I'm stuck choosing between fragile time-window approaches that risk either missing users or double-sending. I'm trying to think if there's a deterministic way to derive eligibility that avoids both duplicates and misses.

For low credits, the real problem is the condition stays true indefinitely until a top-up, so a naive cron would spam the user every run. I'm working out whether I can anchor the "already sent" state to the credit ledger itself — specifically, checking whether the most recent ledger row is the exact one that crossed the threshold, so the email only fires on that transition rather than on every subsequent check.

But detecting the crossing row alone isn't enough since overlapping cron runs within the same time window could still double-send, so I need some durable marker to dedupe against — and writing a zero-delta ledger row won't work since the system explicitly skips logging zero-charge events.

I'm considering other tables that could serve as a generic idempotency store, like a StripeEvent table keyed by a free-form id, which could double as a dedup mechanism without polluting the financial ledger.

I should check the billing webhook to see if it ever enumerates or cleans that table before deciding. Actually, rereading the brief, the intended approach is derivation — figuring out "have we already told this person this?" from existing data like CreditLedger, Build, and Project.publishedAt rather than repurposing StripeEvent, and if an email genuinely can't be made idempotent without a schema change, I should implement it disabled behind a guard and state exactly what schema is needed. For build-failed emails specifically, the natural dedupe key is the Build row itself, one email per failed build — though I still need to figure out how to detect we've already sent it.

I realize something important: since I can only edit lib/notifications and app/api/notifications, nothing currently calls send.ts except the cron endpoint — so welcome/build-failed/published emails should be designed as event-driven inline hooks (exported functions meant to be wired in by the route owners with one line each), which are naturally once-per-occurrence, while the low-credits email remains the cron-driven case that genuinely needs derived idempotency.

For that low-credits case, I'm working out the threshold logic — balance dropping below twice the user's average build credits — and trying to derive idempotency purely from the ledger itself without a separate marker: the rule would be to email only when the latest ledger row shows the balance is currently below threshold AND that row is a spend whose pre-transaction balance was still above threshold, meaning it's the exact moment of crossing into low-credit territory.

But I'm realizing this breaks down with cron timing — if two runs land in the same window or the cron jitters/retries, the same crossing row could trigger duplicate emails, so I need to think about how to anchor the time window more reliably to avoid double-sends.

So the honest conclusion is that for low credits we can only guarantee "at most once per crossing per cron slot," not true exactly-once under retries. I'm wondering if an in-memory guard within the single Node process—like a Map tracking already-notified ledger row IDs—could make duplicates harmless within that process's lifetime, similar to the contact route's rate limiter.

That approach resets on deploy though, so a deploy mid-window could still trigger a resend, but bounded to at most two emails per crossing given the window size and rarity of deploys. Still, repeatedly emailing someone "you're running low" feels like it needs a stronger guarantee than that.

I'm now considering a deterministic slot approach instead: bucket time into fixed windows and only consider crossing rows from the previous complete slot, so retries within the same slot always produce the same candidate set that the in-memory guard can dedupe — leaving only the restart-mid-slot case as a residual risk, which I could close by persisting the guard against the ledger row itself.

I'm settling on this shape: identify the crossing row as the latest ledger entry that dropped the user below threshold, restrict eligibility to the prior complete cron slot, and dedupe in-process for retries — while flagging the residual risk and proposing an `EmailLog`/`NotificationLog` table with a unique (userId, kind, dedupeKey) constraint. I also want to check that users who were already below threshold before this feature existed still get caught on their next genuine crossing, even if they stay low.

That's a deliberate choice to avoid blasting existing low-balance users retroactively. I also want to handle the zero-balance case — still a crossing, but the messaging should shift to something like "not enough for another build" rather than the generic low-credits warning, using a shared template with balance and buildsLeft fields. I should verify the threshold logic matches what the UI shows by checking where `averageBuildCredits` is used elsewhere in the codebase.

For welcome emails, I'm leaning toward exporting `sendWelcomeEmail(userId)` for signup routes to call inline rather than running it through the cron job, since cron-triggered welcome emails wouldn't be idempotent and don't fit the re-engagement pattern described in the brief — it stays implemented but unwired, ready for a one-line integration.

I'm working out how to guard against duplicate sends: checking that `user.createdAt` falls within a short window (like 5 minutes) plus an in-memory once-per-user set gives a reasonably robust inline safeguard without overengineering it. For build-failed emails, I'm planning a similar inline hook, `sendBuildFailedEmail(buildId)`, scoped once per build.

I want this to verify the build's status is FAILED, credits charged is zero, and no ledger row references it before claiming "you weren't charged" — so the email never lies about billing. If a ledger row exists, skip the email; also skip aborted builds where the client just disconnected, since that's noise rather than a real failure worth notifying about. ## The four templates

Composed as a block list rendered to **plain text first**, with the HTML alternative generated from the same blocks — the two literally cannot drift. Inlined CSS only, no images, no web fonts, no pixel, zero network requests on open. All user-supplied strings (project names) are HTML-escaped and control-char stripped; nothing user-controlled ever reaches a header (`to:` is the bare address).

1. **Welcome** — what Kodely builds, three concrete first projects, "500 credits is $1 of underlying cost", the real 120–550 estimate and 750 grant pulled live from `lib/credits.ts` so they can't go stale, link to `/dashboard`, plus a pointer to the spend cap.
2. **Low credits** — states the balance, the runway sentence copied from `CreditMeter`, and the user's own measured average, with a `measured` flag so it says "yours have cost about N" only when they actually have charged builds (otherwise "a typical Kodely build"). Links to `/pricing`.
3. **Build failed** — leads with "You were not charged… no credits left your balance", three concrete things to try. Deliberately carries **no error text** (build errors can quote the user's own source).
4. **Site published** — the live URL, and next steps including the true republish semantics (edits stay in draft until you publish again).

## Idempotency — how each one is solved

The core mechanism: every notification is derived from a **state transition at one instant**, and each run only considers transitions inside one **clock-aligned closed 15-minute slot** `[floor(now,15m)-15m, floor(now,15m))`. Because the slot comes from the wall clock rather than from when the job started, a run at 12:00:03 and a retry at 12:07 compute the identical candidate list; an in-process claim map keyed by occurrence id (ledger row / build / project id) then makes the repeat a no-op.

- **Low credits** — the ledger row that dropped the user a grade. Also requires no newer ledger row exists (a top-up disarms it; a later spend simply defers to its own slot).
- **Welcome** — `User.createdAt` in the slot; happens once by definition, plus a 1-hour age guard in the sender.
- **Build failed** — `Build.endedAt` in the slot, one per user per run, client-disconnect aborts excluded, and skipped if they started another build afterwards (that person is at the keyboard and already handled it).
- **Site published** — `Project.publishedAt` in the slot, restricted to **first** publishes by counting `project.published` Event rows for that project. Republishes send nothing.

**A real finding that changed the design.** A boolean "crossed from fine to low" does not work here. `SIGNUP_GRANT` is 750 and the fallback average is 400, so `CreditMeter` already reads *amber for a brand-new account* (`buildsLeft = 1`). Anyone whose builds cost more than ~375 credits is never on the "fine" side, so the warning would have silently never fired for exactly the cohort it exists for. I graded the state instead — `ok` → `low` → `spent` (can't afford another build, includes zero/negative) — and email on any downward move. Simulated over a whole 750 tank at five different build costs: **always 1 or 2 emails, never a stream**, and never one ten minutes after signup. `creditState` was diff-tested against a re-implementation of the meter's rule across 2,600+ balance/average combinations: zero mismatches.

2. **The schema I'd want.** Everything above is *at-most-once*: a completely skipped cron run drops that slot, and a process restart between two runs covering one slot could resend. A table would make it exactly-once and let me drop both the slot window and the in-memory map:
   ```prisma
   model EmailLog {
     id         String   @id @default(cuid())
     userId     String
     kind       String   // welcome | low_credits | build_failed | site_published
     dedupeKey  String   // ledger row / build / project id
   ```

| `KODELY_CRON_SECRET` | **Required.** Unset, or shorter than 16 chars, and the endpoint 404s. |
| `SMTP_HOST/PORT/USER/PASS`, `MAIL_FROM` | Already used by `lib/mail.ts`; unset = everything inert. |
| `APP_URL`, `KODELY_SITES_BASE` | Already present; link targets. |
| `KODELY_NOTIFY_ALLOWLIST` | Rollout guard — comma-separated addresses, everyone else skipped. **Set this to your own address first.** |
| `KODELY_NOTIFY_DRY_RUN=1` | Compose and log, never touch SMTP. |
| `KODELY_NOTIFY_DISABLED=1` | Master kill switch. |
| `KODELY_NOTIFY_{WELCOME,LOW_CREDITS,BUILD_FAILED,PUBLISHED}_CRON` | Per-kind toggles, all default on. |

## Cron line (prod only)

```
*/15 * * * * curl -fsS -m 120 -X POST https://kodely.me/api/notifications/run -H "x-kodely-cron-secret: $KODELY_CRON_SECRET" >/dev/null
```

More often is harmless; less often drops slots. Secret is header-only (never a query param — it'd land in nginx/CDN logs), compared with `timingSafeEqual` over SHA-256 digests so length doesn't leak either, and a bad secret returns **404**. `?dry=1` gives a read-only rehearsal returning counts only. `MAX_PER_KIND = 200` caps the blast radius per run. Staging must not run this — the published-site URL it builds is the prod wildcard.

## Verified vs assumed

**Verified:** failed builds are genuinely never charged (`app/api/generate/route.ts` writes `creditsCharged: 0` on both failure paths and leaves the ledger untouched) — and the sender re-checks the ledger before making that claim in writing. All four scans run against the local Postgres including the Prisma JSON `props` filter. The full run wrote **nothing** to the DB (row counts identical before/after). No email was sent: SMTP was unset and the allowlist pointed at `nobody@example.invalid`. Auth path tested end-to-end (unset / too-short / missing / wrong / query-param secrets all 404; both valid header forms 200).

**Assumed:** that SMTP delivery works, since I couldn't exercise it. That negative ledger deltas only ever come from builds (true today — rewards and Stripe grants are positive).

**Not built, deliberately:** no re-engagement or drip email for the "signed up and never came back" user. There's no consent record and no unsubscribe mechanism, so that one is marketing, not transactional, and it needs consent tracking we don't have.
